```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggstats)

atus_fmt<-readRDS(here::here('Data/atus.rds'))


```

## Example data

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   Data from the 2024 [American Time Use Survey](https://www.bls.gov/tus/)

-   Conducted annually since 2003.

-   Respondents answer questions about how much of their time is spent performing various activities (childcare, work, school, recreation etc.)

-   I've done some reformatting and aggregation to simplify some analyses.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
library(tidyverse)
library(ggstats)

file<-url("https://github.com/Neilblund/SDSB340-Spring-2026/raw/refs/heads/master/Data/atus.rds")
atus_fmt<-readRDS(file)


```
:::
:::::

## Visualization

### Bad Visuals

![](images/fig-ch-01-holmes-monstrous-only.png){width="100%"}

### Parts of a plot

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
Required components:

::: incremental
1.  Data and mapping: We need to choose what elements we'll be visualizing and how they map onto different parts of the plot (what goes on the x and y axis? If we're color coding, what variables determine colors? Or shapes?)

2.  Layers: the visible representations of the data. The most important being geometries (bar, point, line etc.)

3.  Scales: the mapping from data units to distances, colors, etc.

4.  The remaining elements can be modified, but they're often left at default values (ggplot assumes you want carteesian coordinates unless you say otherwise, for instance)
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/ggplot_parts.png)
:::
::::::

### Dimensionality

-   Data is multi-dimensional, but visuals are 2D.

-   A core challenge for good visualization is elegantly handling this dimensional mismatch by:

    -   simplifying data
    -   color/shape/symbol encoding
    -   faceting

## ggplot

-   Base R already has pretty good support for data visualization, but `ggplot2` is usually easier to pick up and requires less code to do cool stuff.

### ggplot

You'll always start with a call to ggplot

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
On it's own, this just makes empty space.

```{r}

ggplot()

```
:::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
We can add data and aesthetics to control what goes into the space: axes, colors, positions etc.

```{r}

ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(x=t020201))

# equivalent with pipe: 
#atus_fmt|>
#  ggplot(aes(x=t020201))

```
:::
::::
::::::

### ggplot geometry

-   You'll use the `+` to add more layers to a ggplot object.
-   Layers with the prefix `geom_` will give us different plot types: `geom_point()` (scatterplots), `geom_boxplot()` (boxplots), `geom_bar()` (barplots) etc.

### ggplot geometry

You'll use the `+` to add one or more layers to a ggplot object. Layers with the `geom_` prefix will produce different kinds of plots:

:::::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(x=chores)) + 
  geom_histogram()

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_fmt, aes(x=GTMETSTA)) + geom_bar()


```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column


ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(x=chores)) + 
  geom_density() +  # kernel density
  geom_rug() # rug plot



```
:::
::::::

### ggplot scales

We can also change the x or y scaling from the default using `scale_` functions

:::::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(x=chores)) + 
  geom_histogram() 

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(x=chores)) + 
  geom_histogram() + 
  scale_x_log10() # logarithmic scale


```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

label_hours_minutes <- function(x) {
  h <- floor(x / 60)
  m <- round(x %% 60)
  
  # Logic to create strings like "1h 30m", "45m", or "2h"
  labels <- ifelse(h > 0, 
                   paste0(h, "h", ifelse(m > 0, paste0(" ", m, "m"), "")),
                   paste0(m, "m"))
  
  # Ensure NAs remain NAs
  labels[is.na(x)] <- NA
  return(labels)
}

ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(x=chores)) + 
  geom_histogram() + 
  # using a custom label function to show hours and minutes
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_hours_minutes)



```
:::
::::::

### ggplot labels

You can use `labs` to add a title and/or modify the x and y axis labels:

::::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column




ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(x=chores)) + 
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(title = "Time spent doing household chores",
       caption = "Source: American Time Use Survey, 2024",
       x = "Time spent on chores",
       y = "Count"
  )


```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column


ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(x=chores)) + 
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(title = "Time spent doing household chores",
       caption = "Source: American Time Use Survey, 2024",
       x = "Time spent on chores",
       y = "Count"
  )

```
:::
:::::

## Try it out

```{r}

library(tidyverse)

file<-url("https://github.com/Neilblund/SDSB340-Spring-2026/raw/refs/heads/master/Data/atus.rds")
atus_fmt<-readRDS(file)
label_hours_minutes <- function(x) {
  h <- floor(x / 60)
  m <- round(x %% 60)
  
  # Logic to create strings like "1h 30m", "45m", or "2h"
  labels <- ifelse(h > 0, 
                   paste0(h, "h", ifelse(m > 0, paste0(" ", m, "m"), "")),
                   paste0(m, "m"))
  
  # Ensure NAs remain NAs
  labels[is.na(x)] <- NA
  return(labels)
}

```

1.  Create a histogram to show time spent on one of the other activities: `sleep`, `work`, `education`, `travel`, `religious_activities` or `sports_recreation`

2.  Add x and y axis labels, a title, subtitle, and caption.

3.  Pick a [theme](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggtheme.html) and apply it.

4.  Use the `label_hours_minutes` function to format the x-axis.

5.  Assign the result to an object and use the [`ggsave`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggsave.html) function to export it to a file.

## Plotting data multiple dimensions

### Dimensions and color-coding

To capture an additional dimension, you can put another variable on the y-axis

```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(x = chores, y = TUDIARYDAY))  +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Time spent on household chores",
    subtitle = "(by day of the week)",
    x = "Minutes spent on chores",
    y = "Day",
    caption = "Source: American Time Use Survey, 2024",
  ) +
  theme_classic()

```

### Dimensions and color-coding

For additional dimensions beyond 2, you can use `color` or `fill`, `shape`, or `size` in the aesthetics to distinguish groups.

::::::: r-stack
```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(x = chores, y = TUDIARYDAY))  +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Time spent on household chores",
    subtitle = "(by day of the week)",
    x = "Minutes spent on chores",
    y = "Day",
    caption = "Source: American Time Use Survey, 2024",
  ) +
  theme_classic()

```

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column


ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(x = chores,
                             y = TUDIARYDAY, 
                             fill = TESEX,
                             
                             ))  +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Time spent on household chores",
    subtitle = "(by day of the week and sex)",
    x = "Minutes spent on chores",
    y = "Day",
    caption = "Source: American Time Use Survey, 2024",
  )  +
  theme_classic()

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(y= factor(TRCHILDNUM), fill=TESEX, x = chores))  +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Time spent on household chores",
    subtitle = "(by day, number of children, and sex)",
    x = "Minutes spent on chores",
    y = "Number of children",
    fill = "Sex",
    caption = "Source: American Time Use Survey, 2024",
  ) +
  theme_classic()

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(y=TUDIARYDAY, color=TESEX, x = chores))  +
  geom_point(pch = 21, position = position_jitterdodge()) +
  labs(
    title = "Time spent on household chores",
    subtitle = "(by day number of children and sex)",
    x = "Minutes spent on chores",
    y = "Number of children",
    color = "Sex",
    caption = "Source: American Time Use Survey, 2024",
  ) +
  theme_classic()

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(y=TUDIARYDAY, color=TESEX, x = chores))  +
  geom_point(pch = 21, position = position_jitterdodge()) +
  labs(
    title = "Time spent on household chores",
    subtitle = "(by day, number of children, and sex)",
    x = "Minutes spent on chores",
    y = "Number of children",
    color = "Sex",
    caption = "Source: American Time Use Survey, 2024",
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("orange", "lightblue"))

```
:::
:::::::


## Try it out

1. Use boxplots or jittered points to examine the relationship between `TESEX` (sex) and `hh_caretaking` (caring for household members)

2. Use color coding/fills to visualize this relationship by `GTMETSTA` (metropolitan status)

3. Try adding a custom color palette using `scale_fill_manual()` or `scale_color_manual()` (you'll need to pick three color values)


### Aggregation

In a lot of cases, you'll need to do some aggregation in order to get a meaningful visual summary of some relationship. The `stat_summary` functions can automatically aggregate by group:

```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(atus_fmt, aes(x=decade, y = chores, group=1)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", color = "black") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Time spent on chores",
    subtitle = "By age",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Minutes",
    caption = "ATUS: 2024"
  )  + 
  theme_classic()


```

### Aggregation

However, this is a little inflexible, so in many cases it makes sense to do the aggregation step separately.

::::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

atus_agg<-atus_fmt|>
  group_by(decade)|>
  summarise(
            wtd_chores = weighted.mean(x=chores,  
                                       w =TUFINLWGT,
                                       na.rm=T)
            
            )

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=decade, y = wtd_chores, group=1)) +
  geom_line(lwd=1)+
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Average time spent on chores (weighted)",
    subtitle = "By age",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Minutes",
    caption = "ATUS: 2024"
  ) +
  theme_classic()

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column
atus_agg<-atus_fmt|>
  group_by(decade, TESEX)|>
  summarise(
            wtd_chores = weighted.mean(x=chores, 
                                       w =TUFINLWGT, 
                                       na.rm=T)
            )

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=decade, y = wtd_chores, 
                     color=TESEX, 
                     group=TESEX)) +
  geom_line(lwd=1)+
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Average time spent on chores (weighted)",
    subtitle = "(by age and sex)",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Minutes",
    color= 'Sex',
    caption = "ATUS: 2024"
  ) +
  theme_classic() 

```
:::
:::::

### Faceting

Alternatively, faceting with `facet_wrap` or `facet_grid` splits your data into multiple subplots (panels) based on one or more categorical variables.

::::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(x = chores,
                             y = TUDIARYDAY, 
                             fill = TESEX,
                             shape =TESEX
                             ))  +
   
  geom_boxplot(outliers=FALSE) + # removing outliers
  labs(
     title = "Time spent on household chores",
    subtitle = "(by sex, day, and cohabitation)",
    x = "Minutes spent on chores",
    y = "Day of the week",
    caption = "ATUS: 2024",
    fill = "Sex", # Adjusting color legend title
    shape = "Sex" # Adjusting shape legend title
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  facet_wrap(~TRSPPRES)

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(data  = atus_fmt, aes(x = chores,
                             y = TUDIARYDAY, 
                             fill = TESEX))  +
  geom_boxplot(outliers=FALSE) +
  labs(
 title = "Time spent on household chores",    
 subtitle = "(by sex, day, cohabitation, and metro status)",
    x = "Minutes spent on chores",
    y = "Day of the week",
    caption = "ATUS: 2024",
    fill = "Sex" # Adjusting the legend title
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  # row var ~ column var
  facet_grid(GTMETSTA ~TRSPPRES)

```
:::
:::::

### Long data

-   ggplot works best with long format data. If we want to visualize several variables at once, you'll often need to do some additional data wrangling.

### Long data

:::::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

# store the variable labels in a list
labels<-lapply(atus_fmt, function(x) attr(x, "label"))|>
  unlist()
# make long format data
time_long<-atus_fmt|>
  # selecting only the weight + columns related to activities
  select(sleep:travel, TUFINLWGT)|>
  # pivoting everything except the weights
  pivot_longer(cols=-TUFINLWGT)|>
  # adding the labels as a new column
  mutate(label = labels[name])

# viewing the results
time_long|>
  slice_head(n=10)

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

time_aggregate<-time_long|>
  group_by(label)|>
  summarize(avg = weighted.mean(value, w=TUFINLWGT))
ggplot(time_aggregate, aes(x = avg, y=label)) + geom_point()



```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

time_aggregate<-time_long|>
  group_by(label)|>
  summarize(avg = weighted.mean(value, w=TUFINLWGT))|>
  mutate(label = reorder(label, avg))

ggplot(time_aggregate, aes(x = avg, y=label)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
 title = "Average time spent on different activities",    
    x = "Time spent",
    y = "",
    caption = "ATUS: 2024"  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_hours_minutes) +
  theme_bw()



```
:::
::::::

### Faceting and scaling

Big differences in the scaling can make it difficult to identify *relative* changes within each group. Faceting with "free" axes can be a useful way to highlight a change at the expense of distorting absolute values.

### Faceting and scaling

::::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
This plot shows hours spent on different activities by age using the same scale for each facet.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true


time_long<-atus_fmt|>
  mutate(weekend = !TUDIARYDAY %in% c("Saturday", "Sunday"))|>
  select(sleep:travel, TEAGE, TUFINLWGT, weekend)|>
  pivot_longer(cols=-c(TUFINLWGT, weekend, TEAGE))|>
  mutate(label = labels[name])

time_aggregate<-time_long|>
  group_by(label, weekend, TEAGE)|>
  summarize(avg = weighted.mean(value, w=TUFINLWGT))


ggplot(time_aggregate, aes(x = TEAGE, y =avg, 
                           color=weekend,
                           group=weekend)) +
  geom_point(size=.1) +
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Average time spent on different activities",    
    x = "Time spent",
    y = "",
    caption = "ATUS: 2024"  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_hours_minutes) +
  theme_bw() +
  facet_wrap(~label)



```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Here's what it looks like using a "free" y scale:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true

time_long<-atus_fmt|>
  mutate(weekend = !TUDIARYDAY %in% c("Saturday", "Sunday"))|>
  select(sleep:travel, TEAGE, TUFINLWGT, weekend)|>
  pivot_longer(cols=-c(TUFINLWGT, weekend, TEAGE))|>
  mutate(label = labels[name])

time_aggregate<-time_long|>
  group_by(label, weekend, TEAGE)|>
  summarize(avg = weighted.mean(value, w=TUFINLWGT))


ggplot(time_aggregate, aes(x = TEAGE, y =avg, 
                           color=weekend,
                           group=weekend)) +
  geom_point(size=.1) +
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Average time spent on different activities",    
    x = "Time spent",
    y = "",
    caption = "ATUS: 2024"  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_hours_minutes) +
  theme_bw() +
  facet_wrap(~label, 
             # Free scale on the y-axis
             scales='free_y')



```
:::
:::::

## Survey data

Some special considerations for survey visualization:

-   Visualizations for categorical data
-   Visualizing weighted responses
-   Handling over-plotting
-   Visualizing the margin of error
-   Visualizing the results from a model

### Survey data: Categorical Responses and Weights

-   Many survey variables are categorical rather than continuous, which can restrict our options for visualization.

#### Survey data: Bar plots

::::::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
`geom_bar` automatically creates bars proportional to the number of observations.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_fmt, aes(x=GTMETSTA)) + 
  geom_bar()

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
`geom_col` creates bars that are proportional to a value in the data (so you need to create the aggregated data yourself)

```{r}
#| output-location: column

atus_agg<-atus_fmt|>
  group_by(GTMETSTA)|>
  summarise(Count = n())

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=GTMETSTA, y= Count)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  theme_bw()




```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Doing the aggregation separately offers better flexibility for calculations and formatting.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

atus_agg<-atus_fmt|>
  group_by(GTMETSTA)|>
  summarise(count = sum(TUFINLWGT))|>
  mutate(proportion = count /sum(count))

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=GTMETSTA, y=proportion)) + 
  geom_col() +
  theme_bw()

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Creating a dumbbell plot using `geom_pointrange` can be an appealing alternative to bar plots that focuses more attention on the important stuff (the ends)

```{r}
#| output-location: column

atus_agg<-atus_fmt|>
  group_by(GTMETSTA)|>
  summarise(count = sum(TUFINLWGT))|>
  mutate(proportion = count /sum(count))

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=GTMETSTA, y=proportion)) + 
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = 0, ymax = proportion),
                  # making wider lines 
                  lwd=.7, 
                  # increasing the point size
                  size = 1.5)

```
:::
:::::::

#### Survey data: Two-way bar plots

::::::::: r-stack
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| output-location: column

atus_agg<-atus_fmt|>
  group_by(telework, PEEDUCA)|>
  summarise(count = sum(TUFINLWGT))|>
  ungroup()|>
  drop_na()|>
  group_by(PEEDUCA)|>
  mutate(proportion = count /sum(count))

atus_agg

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
In this instance, the axis labels are too long to fit on the page.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=PEEDUCA, 
                     y=proportion, 
                     fill=telework)) + 
  geom_col()

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Using `coord_flip` (or just reversing what goes on the x and y axis) is often an easy fix in this situation.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=PEEDUCA, 
                     y=proportion, 
                     fill=telework)) + 
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
Adding `position='dodge'` to the plot will give side-by-side columns, instead of stacked bars.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=PEEDUCA, 
                     y=proportion, 
                     fill=telework)) + 
  coord_flip()+
  geom_col(position='dodge')
  

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
`scales::label_percent()` will automatically turn proportions into formatted % tick marks:

```{r}
#| output-location: column

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=PEEDUCA, 
                     y=proportion, 
                     fill=telework)) + 
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()+
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent())+
  labs(x = "Education",
       y = "Percent",
       fill  = "Telework"
       )

```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out}
You can also simplify the calculation of weighted proportions here using the `srvyr` package.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

library(srvyr)
atus_svy<-atus_fmt|>
  as_survey_design(weights = TUFINLWGT)

# getting survey proportions
atus_agg<-atus_svy|>
  # drop missing values
  drop_na(telework, PEEDUCA)|>
  # get proportions summing to 100% by education
  group_by(PEEDUCA, telework)|>
  summarise(survey_prop(vartype = 'ci'))

ggplot(atus_agg, aes(x=PEEDUCA, 
                     y=coef, 
                     fill=telework)) + 
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()+
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent())+
  labs(x = "Education",
       y = "Percent",
       fill  = "Telework"
       )

```
:::
:::::::::

#### Survey data: Likert Plots

Visualizing Likert scales can offer some unique challenges and there are multiple R packages with purpose-built Likert visualization

#### Survey data: Likert Plots

Here's an example of a Likert scale plot using regular ggplot functions.

```{r}
#| output-location: column

fname<-here::here("data", "anes_timeseries_2024_csv_20250808.zip")
anes  <- read_csv(unz(fname,"anes_timeseries_2024_csv_20250808.csv"))|>
  # removing people who didn't complete the post interview survey
  filter(V240002c == 2)
anes <- anes|>
  mutate(
    respect_elders = recode_values(V242260, 
                                   1 ~ 0 , 
                                   2 ~ 1),
    good_manners = recode_values(V242261, 
                                 1 ~ 0, 
                                 2 ~ 1),
    obedience = recode_values(V242262, 
                              2 ~ 0, 
                              1 ~ 1),
    well_behaved = recode_values(V242263, 
                                 1 ~ 0, 
                                 2 ~ 1),
    authoritarianism = respect_elders + good_manners + obedience + well_behaved
  )

anes$authoritarianism_factor<-factor(anes$authoritarianism, 
                                     levels=c(0, 1, 2,3,4),
                                     labels=c("Lowest", "Low", "Moderate", "High", "Highest")
                                     )
labs<-c("1. Strongly agree",
"2. Somewhat agree",
"3. Neither agree nor disagree",
"4. Somewhat disagree",
"5. Strongly disagree")
levs<-c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

anes$prefer_stronglead <- factor(anes$V242411, levels=levs, labels=labs)
anes$gender<-factor(anes$V241550, levels=c(1,2), labels=c("Male", "Female"))

summary_data <- anes |>
  group_by(gender, prefer_stronglead, authoritarianism_factor) |>
  summarize(n = n()) |>
  drop_na()|>
  group_by(authoritarianism_factor, gender)|>
  mutate(total = sum(n),
         proportion = n/total,
         label = sprintf("%.0f%%",
                         proportion*100,
                         n)
         )


ggplot(summary_data, aes(y=proportion, 
                         x=authoritarianism_factor, 
                         fill=prefer_stronglead, label=label)) +
  geom_bar(stat='identity', position='stack') +
  facet_grid(rows=~gender) +
  scale_fill_discrete(palette = "RdYlBu") +
  geom_text(position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5))+
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Authoritarianism index",
       y= "%",
       fill = 'Preference for strong leader',
       title = 'V242411: A strong leader in government is good for the United States\neven if the leader bends the rules to get things done',
       subtitle = '(by authoritarianism and gender)',
       caption = 'Source: ANES 2024'
       ) 

```

#### Survey data: Likert Plots

Here's an example of creating a likert plot using the `gglikert` function from `ggstats`.

```{r}
#| output-location: column



anes|>
  drop_na(prefer_stronglead, gender, authoritarianism_factor)|>
  gglikert(
         include = c(prefer_stronglead),
         facet_rows = vars(authoritarianism_factor),
         # separate results by gender
         facet_cols =vars(gender),
         # removing the label so this can be printed in the title
         variable_labels = c(prefer_stronglead = "") 
         ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
    labs(
       fill = 'Preference for strong leader',
       title = 'V242411: A strong leader in government is good for the United States\neven if the leader bends the rules to get things done',
       subtitle = '(by authoritarianism and gender)',
       caption = 'Source: ANES 2024'
       ) 

```
